title: A study to test a home walking programme for people living with peripheral artery disease
official: The MOtivating Structured walking Activity in Intermittent Claudication (MOSAIC2) feasibility study
summary:
Background and study aims 
One in five older people has narrowing in their leg arteries (called peripheral artery disease). This causes poor circulation and pain when walking (called intermittent claudication). Walking frequently is the best way to improve this pain and reduce the risk of other health problems or severe artery disease. Unfortunately, it is hard for people to walk on their own when they are in pain. To help with this, the study team worked with patients and practitioners to design and test a new home walking exercise programme with regular physiotherapist support. It was called MOtivating Structured walking Activity in Intermittent Claudication (MOSAIC1; https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN14501418). When delivered in hospitals, it improved people's walking capacity and was acceptable and valued by both patients and providers. This intervention has now been adapted so it can be provided in GP practices and community services by a broader range of providers. This adapted 3-month programme will be called MOSAIC2. 
The study team will now see if MOSAIC2 works, whether it is value for money for the NHS and how it can be rolled out. This feasibility study is the first phase of the research that will answer these questions. The feasibility study will assess whether MOSAIC2 can be provided in GP practices and community services well and help us design a larger trial.

Who can participate? 
Patients aged at least 50 years with intermittent claudication.

What does the study involve? 
Participants will be recruited from GP practices or community trusts over 6 months. The study team will train practitioners to deliver MOSAIC2. They will assess patients’ activity at home, do walking and health tests and ask some questionnaires before and after completing the MOSAIC2 programme. They will also invite some patients and practitioners to give feedback on the MOSAIC2 programme and our study processes. The findings will be summarised to see if the MOSAIC2 programme or the trial plans need adapting.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants may benefit from increased motivation, improved walking capacity, and better mobility to support daily activities. The findings will also help research design a larger trial to improve care for people with peripheral artery disease in the NHS. The risks are low. Participants may experience mild muscle aches, soreness, or cramps as they increase their walking activity, as well as a small risk of falls while exercising at home. To minimise these risks, participants received support from a trained healthcare professional who will tailor the walking plan to their individual ability. 

Where is the study run from?  
The study is sponsored by City St George’s, University of London, and coordinated by the Leicester Clinicals Trials Unit, University of Leicester. This walking programme will take place across six GP practice and community health trusts across England, Scotland and Wales.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
September 2026 to June 2027

Who is funding the study? 
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Prof. Lindsay Bearne, lbearne@citystgeorges.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults aged 50 years or older 
2. Established PAD recorded in medical records based on:
2.1. Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) of 0.90 or less
2.2. Radiographic evidence of PAD or 
2.3. Clinician-reported diagnosis of PAD 
2.4. People with an ABPI >0.90 will be enrolled if there is other evidence of PAD (e.g., clinical diagnosis; radiographic evidence of PAD determined by the consulting clinician, toe pressure <70 mmHg or toe brachial index ratio of <0.60 if asymptomatic or <0.70 if symptomatic)
3. Symptomatic leg pain defined by one of the following: 
3.1. Ischaemic leg symptoms identified using the self-reported San Diego Claudication Questionnaire
3.2. Interview with potential participant about presence and nature of leg symptoms during walking activity
4. Sufficient grasp of the English language to participate in a dialogue- based intervention 
5. Ability to participate in the trial and provide informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. From Read code search of primary/community care records: Major amputation, wheelchair confinement, having a foot ulcer or critical limb ischaemia 
1. From Read code search of primary/community care records: housebound; terminal illness; > 3 falls in previous year; dementia or significant cognitive impairment, psychotic illness; registered blind; new onset chest pain, myocardial infarction, coronary artery bypass graft or angioplasty within the last 3 months 
3. From Read code search of primary/community care records: Major surgery including individuals that have had lower extremity revascularisation (and now have normal ABPI) or orthopaedic surgery (that still compromises walking ability) during the prior 3 months or anticipated in the next 6 months 
4. Those without self-reported ischaemic leg symptoms during walking or having a walking limitation for a self-reported reason other than PAD or anticipate having major surgery or orthopaedic surgery affecting walking ability in the next 6 months
5. Self-reported completion of any medically prescribed supervised exercise intervention or exercise trial in the previous 3 months or planned participation in prescribed supervised exercise in the next 6 months
